newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bangemann opposes BSE food safety plans.
newsitem.headline: Bangemann opposes BSE food safety plans.

text.p: Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann says he challenges the wisdowm of creating a single consumer controlled department for food safety in the wake of the mad cow crisis.

In an interview with Reuters, Bangemann also criticised a European Parliament committee of inquiry report which attacked the Commission for mishandling the crisis which erupted in March 1996 when Britain said people could catch the fatal disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE)).
"I would not rule out the possibility that the BSE experience will lead to some changes of responsibility between the different Commission services concerned," Bangemann said.
"However, I am not sure that combining all responsibilities for food in a single department is the correct solution."
The current approach with responsibilities divided between several services included checks and balances which could be lost if all responsibilities were given to a single department, he added.

The committee's report voted through the parliament's agriculture committee this week fell short of censuring the European Commission although that could be done when the report is put to the full parliament in Strasbourg on February 19.
The report demands a shake-up of the Commission's services to provide greater control over food safety and a reduction in member states' powers over food and consumer controls.
But the German Commissioner, while recognising that the issue is "difficult", pointed out that the Commission structure reflects those in all member states.

"Moreover, although the American Food and Drug Administration is frequently held up as a model for Europe, I would point out that other departments also have responsibility for food safety issues," he said, noting that the Food Safety Inspection Service comes under the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
In contrast to the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into BSE, the Commissioner rejects accusations that the crisis was mishandled at all levels.

"Many of the criticisms being made now have the benefit of hindsight. No doubt there are lessons which we can all learn from the affair. I sincerely hope that it will be possible to do so without unnecessary rancour or recriminations," he said.
The supply of food in the European Union is safe but there is no room for complacency, food safety rules must be properly enforced, he added.
"Likewise, one point on which I think there is total agreement is that any system of food safety regulation must cover the entire food chain from the farmyard to the table," he said.
"There is little point in regulating certain aspects of food production if unsafe food can be introduced at other points in the production chain," he added.
He criticised member states for their attitude to Commission proposals.

"In the particular case of BSE I must point out that the Commission has, on a number of occasions, recommended or proposed stricter measures which have not been accepted by member states," he said. "Indeed, at the end of last year a proposal to prevent certain tissues from cattle, sheep and goats from entering the food chain was rejected by 10 member states."
The European Union market for food is worth 500,000 million Ecus annually and every household spends 20 per cent of its disposable income on food.
"It is clear that the government control authorities cannot verify every batch of every product which is placed on the market," Bangemann said.
"The primary responsibility to ensure that only safe food is placed on the market must lie with producers and industry," he stressed.
